description: We are an enthusiastic team participating in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, working on the 'Flame in Freefall' challenge to build AI-powered fire safety insights for microgravity environments."
summary: Flame in Freefall is an AI-powered microgravity fire-safety analytics and risk-prediction application developed by Team FireFall AI. In orbital microgravity (~0 g), buoyancy disappears, transforming flames into spherical diffusion-controlled structures that are highly sensitive to oxygen enrichment and low-speed cabin ventilation. Built with Python, Streamlit, and scikit-learn, our interactive tool combines a combustion physics engine—calibrated to NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI), NASA-STD-6001B, and NASA Saffire benchmarks—with a 200-tree Random Forest classifier (87.3% hold-out accuracy) to categorize cabin environments into Low, Moderate, High, or Critical fire-risk tiers. It identifies two critical spacecraft safety boundaries: a steep fire-risk escalation above 35% oxygen concentration and a peak flame-spread zone at 5–10 cm/s ventilation airflow. By enabling real-time What-If atmospheric screening and custom CSV evaluation, Flame in Freefall helps mission designers prevent catastrophic spacecraft fires during future lunar and deep-space habitats.
details: What It Does & How It Works: Flame in Freefall is an interactive microgravity fire-safety decision-support application built with Python and Streamlit. It evaluates 600 simulated combustion runs (or user-uploaded experimental CSV datasets) across five spacecraft cabin variables: total pressure (20.0–101.3 kPa), oxygen concentration (15.0–40.0% O2), ambient temperature (290–400 K), ventilation airflow velocity (0–30 cm/s), and gravity regimes (0 g microgravity, 0.16 g Lunar, and 0.38 g Martian). Using pressure-dependent Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) cutoffs and forced-flow flame-spread equations, the engine computes a 0–100 composite risk score and trains a 200-tree Random Forest classifier (achieving 87.3% hold-out accuracy) to predict Low, Moderate, High, or Critical fire risk in real time. Key Findings & Benefits: 1. Oxygen Danger Threshold: Fire risk escalates sharply above 35% O2, where over 50% of simulated runs enter High or Critical danger tiers. 2. Ventilation Airflow Peak: Unlike Earth fires, microgravity flame spread peaks non-monotonically at 1.92 cm/s inside the 5–10 cm/s low-speed cabin ventilation band before convective cooling reduces spread at higher speeds. 3. Habitat Atmosphere Screening: Evaluates standard ISS-like cabins (101.3 kPa, 21% O2 — Low risk) alongside low-pressure exploration habitats (70.3 kPa / 26.5% O2 and 56.5 kPa / 34.0% O2), flagging elevated High/Critical probabilities (up to 26%). Intended Impact: Provides spacecraft environmental engineers, mission planners, and aerospace researchers with an accessible, fast screening tool to test cabin atmospheres, optimize ventilation placement, and prevent fire hazards on the ISS, Lunar Gateway, and Mars habitats. Tools, Languages & Software Used: - Programming Language: Python 3 - Web Framework & UI: Streamlit - Data Science & Physics Modeling: NumPy, Pandas - Machine Learning: scikit-learn (RandomForestClassifier) - Scientific Visualization: Matplotlib (with visible AI watermarks) Creativity & Factors Considered: Our team bridged fundamental combustion physics (buoyancy loss, spherical diffusion flames, and LOI extinction boundaries) with interpretable machine learning (Gini feature importance confirming O2 drives 57% of risk variance). We also incorporated class-weight balancing for rare Critical events, custom CSV upload validation, and strict transparency disclosures for both NASA datasets and Generative AI assistance.
